A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Riemannian min-max study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison; relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v2 reports original deterministic convergence simulations and Wasserstein GAN experiments on Gaussian data, MNIST digit 0, and Fashion-MNIST T-shirts, including appendix results.

after.justification: v3 retains original simulations and GAN results and adds experiments on all ten classes of MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, plus parameter-sensitivity results.

M1.justification: The GDA and SGA update rules, asymptotic SGA approximation, and stochastic gradient estimator remain unchanged. The smooth DCGAN generator, scattering discriminator, and Stiefel geometry described in v3 were already present in v2, including its appendices.

E1.justification: v3 adds unconditional image modeling over all ten classes of MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, substantially broadening the target distributions beyond digit 0 and T-shirts. It retains both single-class experiments, Gaussian modeling, and the deterministic example.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison methods remain GDA, SGA, and asymptotic SGA in the deterministic example. The new full-dataset experiments reuse GDA and SGA. Alternating GDA remains an initialization procedure; cited extragradient and Hamiltonian methods do not become evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: For retained single-class results, v2 Tables 2–3 become v3 Tables 3 and 5 with GDA budgets revised from 200,000 to 20,000 iterations and SGA budgets from 1–3 million to 100,000–300,000. Reported learning rates for retained timing plots also change. These are documented setting revisions, without establishing reruns. New full-dataset protocols use batch size 512, and Figure 1(c) replaces objective value with approximate distance to equilibrium.

E4.justification: v3 adds a correction-strength sensitivity study over theta from 0.01 to 0.5 at fixed tau = 5 (Appendix N.2, Figure 5). New timing analyses expose delayed GDA instability and a case where GDA is faster than SGA (Figures 4 and 6). Figure 1(c) supplies a direct convergence diagnostic through distance to the known equilibrium. These broaden the earlier tau sweeps and timing analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix M.7 newly specifies that test FID is computed without resampling. Ten resamplings for training/validation FID and for the objective and angle, with sampling standard deviations, were already described in v2. Neither version reports uncertainty across independent training seeds.

E6.justification: v3 Tables 2 and 4 add full-dataset results, including SGA validation FID of 7.6 ± 0.08 on MNIST and 16.6 ± 0.1 on Fashion-MNIST at 500,000 iterations. Section 4.2 changes the Gaussian covariance error at tau = 100 from approximately 0.3 to 0.2. The single-class table scores are retained under revised reported budgets, so they do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 corrects the step-size bound denominator from absolute eigenvalue to squared absolute eigenvalue and specifies negative real parts. Definition 3.1 and the Ostrowski proof distinguish the invariant neighborhood from its geodesically convex subset. Theorem 3.3 additionally gives an explicit step size and rate bound at tau = 1, supported in Appendix I. These revise central formal guarantees.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements more carefully attribute SGA rate guarantees to its asymptotic approximation. The conclusion narrows the suggested convergence to DSE from existing GAN algorithms generally to the chosen GDA initialization algorithms. The principal contributions remain local convergence theory and its illustrative GAN application.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly acknowledges that the attraction-region size and suitable initialization remain uncharacterized. Appendix N.2 adds explanations involving insufficient correction and amplified stochastic noise, plus a tentative global-convergence interpretation. The efficiency discussion now acknowledges that SGA can be slower on full Fashion-MNIST, refining the earlier account of its practical benefits.

D1.justification: v2 promises future PyTorch software, whereas v3 supplies a project repository address; its contents were not inspected. Appendix M adds dataset counts and initialization details, including previously unspecified T-shirt splits and pretraining. Appendix N.2 discloses that theta was tuned on MNIST digit 0 and transferred to other datasets. These materially expand reproducibility information.

R1.justification: v3 adds Benaim and Miclo (2024) to the introduction and bibliography and explicitly attributes the expanded Theorem 3.3 to Jin et al. and Zhang et al. The related-work comparison and overall positioning against existing Riemannian optimization methods remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 edits the abstract, introduction, mathematical explanations, and empirical narrative. It moves notation into Appendix A, relocates the digit-0 discussion to Appendix N.2, and separates experimental details from supplementary results into Appendices M and N. The five-section main structure and most theoretical exposition are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds two full-dataset result tables and Figures 4–6. Figure 1(c) becomes a logarithmic distance-to-equilibrium plot, and Figure 1(b) is redrawn. The retained single-class tables are relocated, with the T-shirt table changed from stacked to side-by-side comparisons. The original timing panels reappear as Figure 7, substantially reorganizing the empirical displays.

improvement.justification: v3 corrects a consequential step-size formula and repairs the local-stability formulation underlying its convergence results. Full-dataset experiments, correction-strength sensitivity evidence, and more complete reproducibility information substantially strengthen the paper beyond its earlier single-class demonstrations. The unexplained iteration-count revisions and speculative global-convergence suggestion remain limitations, but the improvements to mathematical rigor and empirical support provide a clear net gain.
